title: 15 — Design a File Sync Service (Google Drive)
html:
15 — Design a File Sync Service (Google Drive)

The one idea: split every file into blocks, store blocks by content hash, and sync only the blocks that changed. Blocks live in cheap object storage; metadata (files, versions, block lists) lives in a strongly consistent relational DB, because two clients disagreeing about which version is current is the one bug users never forgive.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Upload/download files, sync across devices, see revisions, share files, notifications on edit/delete/share.
  • Web and mobile; any file type; files ≤ 10 GB; encrypted at rest.
  • 50M signed-up users, 10M DAU; 10 GB free each.

Estimates

  • Storage: 50M × 10 GB = 500 PB allocated.
  • Uploads: 2 files/user/day × 500 KB avg → 10M × 2 ÷ 10^5 ≈ ~240 uploads/s, peak ~480/s.

Non-functional: reliability (data loss is unacceptable), fast sync, low bandwidth, scalability, availability.

Step 2 — High-level design

Start from one server (web + DB + /drive/{namespace} on disk), then scale: move files to object storage (replicated across regions), add a load balancer and more web servers, move metadata to a replicated/sharded DB.

APIs

  • POST /files/upload?uploadType=resumable — simple or resumable upload.
  • GET /files/download?path=...
  • GET /files/list_revisions?path=...&limit=20
---
title: File sync — high-level architecture
---
flowchart TB
    U["Client"] --> BS["Block servers<br/>(split, compress, encrypt)"]
    BS --> CS[("Cloud storage<br/>(blocks by hash)")]
    CS --> Cold[("Cold storage")]
    U --> LB["Load balancer"] --> API["API servers"]
    API --> MC[("Metadata cache")]
    API --> MDB[("Metadata DB")]
    API --> NS["Notification service<br/>(long polling)"]
    NS --> U2["Other clients"]
    API --> OBQ["Offline backup queue"]
  • Block servers split files into blocks (e.g. 4 MB), compress, encrypt, upload; each block has a hash ID.
  • Metadata DB: users, files, blocks, versions.
  • Notification service: tells other clients a file changed.
  • Offline backup queue: changes for offline clients, pulled when they reconnect.

Sync conflicts

Two users edit the same file at once: first version processed wins; the other gets a conflict — keep both copies (file (conflicted copy).docx) and let the user merge.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Block servers — the two optimisations

  1. Delta sync: on change, only modified blocks are uploaded (rolling hash / content-defined chunking finds unchanged blocks even when bytes shift).
  2. Compression per block, algorithm by file type (gzip/bzip2 for text; media already compressed).

Dedup: blocks with the same hash stored once — across versions, and optionally across users.

3.2 Strong consistency for metadata

Cache and DB replicas must agree:

  • Invalidate cache on DB write; keep replicas consistent.
  • Use a relational DB with ACID — metadata is small and relational; NoSQL would need consistency built by hand.

3.3 Metadata schema

user          (user_id, name, email, …)
device        (device_id, user_id, last_logged_in_at, push_id)
namespace     (namespace_id, root_dir, owner)
file          (file_id, namespace_id, file_name, relative_path, is_directory, latest_version, checksum, created_at, …)
file_version  (id, file_id, device_id, version_number, last_modified)   -- read-only history
block         (block_id, file_version_id, block_order, hash)

3.4 Upload flow

Two requests in parallel: add metadata (status = pending, notify others) and upload file (block servers → cloud storage → on completion, callback marks status uploaded, notify others).

3.5 Download flow

Notification arrives (or client polls on reconnect) → fetch metadata → get changed block list → download blocks from block servers → reconstruct file.

3.6 Notification service

Long polling (Dropbox's choice): notifications are one-way and infrequent, so WebSocket's bidirectionality isn't needed. Client holds a long-poll connection; on change, it closes and the client fetches metadata.

3.7 Saving storage

  • Dedupe blocks (hash).
  • Limit versions kept and weight recent ones more.
  • Move old/inactive data to cold storage.

3.8 Failure handling

Failure Handling
LB Secondary takes over (heartbeats)
Block server Other servers pick up pending jobs
Cloud storage Multi-region replication
API server Stateless; LB reroutes
Metadata cache Replicated; replace node
Metadata DB primary Promote a replica
Notification server Clients reconnect to another (slow — many connections to re-establish)
Offline backup queue Replicated; consumers resubscribe

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Alternative: upload directly from client to cloud storage (faster, but chunking/compression/encryption logic must live in every client, and clients are easier to tamper with). Moving presence out of the notification service to its own service is another option.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Blocks: Blob Storage with content-hash names; immutability policies and soft delete for protection; lifecycle management to cool/archive tiers.
  • Resumable upload: block blobs (StageBlockAsync per 4 MB chunk, CommitBlockListAsync) — Blob Storage already implements block-level upload.
  • Metadata: Azure SQL (ACID, temporal tables give file version history for free).
  • Notifications: SignalR / long polling endpoint; Service Bus for the offline backup queue.
  • Encryption: storage service encryption at rest by default; customer-managed keys in Key Vault.
  • Client side: System.IO.Hashing for fast block hashing; FileSystemWatcher to detect local changes.

Review checklist

  • Block-level storage, delta sync, dedupe by hash.
  • Metadata in a strongly consistent relational store.
  • Schema with file → version → blocks.
  • Upload and download flows in parallel steps.
  • Conflict strategy.
  • Long polling for notifications, justified.
